sentences.text: Omphalosaurus is an extinct genus of marine reptile that lived from the Early Triassic to the Middle Triassic.
Knowledge of this animal primarily comes from fossilized jaw fragments, ribs, and vertebrae.
It was a moderately large and plump marine reptile reaching 5 meters in length and weighing over 783 kilograms.
The creature possessed button-like teeth with dome shapes and circular crowns featuring an enamel surface that looked like orange peel.
Individual teeth were no larger than 12mm in diameter and were arranged in plates on the premaxilla and dentary bones at 90-degree angles.
Its vertebrae lacked the neural arch found atop the centra.
The first fossil was discovered in 1902 in Nevada by V. C. Osmont and formally described in 1906 by John C. Merriam.
A specimen named O. wolfi was found in the Northern Alps on Dürrnberg Mountain within the Lercheck Limestone formation by G. Wolf in 1991 and formally described by Tichy in 1995.
A left humerus of an Omphalosaurus species was found in the Hohenlohe beds of the Garnberg Quarry in Franconia, Germany, by Hagdorn in 1984 and described by Sander and Faber in 1998.
Omphalosaurus was a durophagous animal, adapted to eat hard-shelled prey.
Researchers Sander and Faber hypothesized that Omphalosaurus used fleshy cheeks and suction feeding to grind through hard shells despite lacking grasping dentition.
Recent evidence suggests Omphalosaurus primarily hunted ammonites rather than bivalves.
Based on the Schaumkalk beds at Rüdersdorf, O. peyeri likely inhabited a coastal environment.
Omphalosaurus is classified in the Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Chordata, Class Sauropsida, Superorder Ichthyopterygia, Order Ichthyosauria, and Family Omphalosauridae.
The genus Omphalosaurus was established by Merriam in 1906.
Known species of Omphalosaurus include O. nevadanus, O. nettarhynchus, O. peyeri, O. wolfi, and O. merriami.
The type species of Omphalosaurus is Omphalosaurus nevadanus, and its parent group is the family Omphalosauridae.
Kuhn identified Omphalosaurus as an ichthyosaur in 1934, and Mazin justified this classification in 1983.
Omphalosaurus shares the rare microunit enamel structure in mature teeth found in Ichthyosaurs, supporting its classification within Ichthyosauria.
Fossils of Omphalosaurus have been found in the western United States, Poland, Austria, and Spitsbergen.
O. nevadanus lived during the Middle Triassic Anisian stage.
The species O. peyeri lived during the Middle Anisian period.
Omphalosaurus is an extinct marine reptile from the Triassic found in Nevada, Germany, and Spitsbergen.
Motani argued in 1997 and 2000 that Omphalosaurus belonged to Sauropterygia rather than Ichthyopterygia due to a lack of specific ichthyosaur traits.
The placement of teeth is the most controversial feature regarding the classification of Omphalosaurus.
Sander and Faber suggested O. wolfi might be O. cf. nevadanus, but Maisch argued it should remain a distinct species pending further investigation.
Fossils from Spitsbergen described by Wiman in 1910 were initially considered Pessopteryx nisseri but now include jaw fragments attributed to O. merriami.
Some researchers regard Pessopteryx nisseri as a separate species or even a distinct genus based on its limb and pectoral girdle fossils.
Sander et al. (2026) classified Pessopteryx nisseri as belonging to the genus Omphalosaurus.
Omphalosaurus was generally considered an ichthyopterygian until Motani (2000) showed it lacked basal synapomorphies of the group.
Maisch (2010) described a new species and re-established the affinity of Omphalosaurus with Ichthyosauria.
